4.
Approximate decomposition into path coverings

In this section we use Corollary
3.6
to turn fractional decompositions provided by Theorem
3.4
into approximate decompositions of almost vertex-regular
k
-graphs into almost spanning collections of paths.
These collections of paths form the basis for the construction of cycle factors in Section
6
.

We need to keep track of how
k
-sets that may be edges in a larger graph are distributed with respect to the paths constructed below.
Suppose
H
is a
k
-graph on
n
vertices with vertex set
V
and
\mathcal{P}
is a collection of paths in
H
.
Let
\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}
.
We use the following terminology to classify
\mathbf{e}
with respect to
\mathcal{P}
, where we often tacitly assume that the collection of paths with respect to which we classify a
k
-set is obvious from the context.
We say that
\mathbf{e}
is

(i)

j
-ending
(or of type
j
-end
) if
j
is the maximal integer for which there is a
j
-set
\mathbf{x}\subseteq\mathbf{e}
and a path
P\in\mathcal{P}
such that
\mathbf{x}
is an end-set of
P
;

(ii)

ending
if it is
j
-ending for some
j\in[k]
;

(iii)

leftover
(or of type
lo
) if it is neither ending nor a subset of
V(\mathcal{P})
;

(iv)

j
-concentrated
(or of type
j
-con
) if it is neither ending nor leftover and
j
is the maximal integer for which there is a
j
-set
\mathbf{x}\subseteq\mathbf{e}
and a path
P\in\mathcal{P}
such that
\mathbf{x}\subseteq V(P)
;

(v)

concentrated
if it is
j
-concentrated for some
j\in[k]
.

We denote the set of types by
\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{T}_{\textup{end}}\cup\{\textup{lo}\}\cup\mathcal{T}_{\textup{con}}
where
\mathcal{T}_{\textup{end}}=\{\textup{$1$-end},\dots,\textup{$k$-end}\}
and
\mathcal{T}_{\textup{con}}=\{\textup{$1$-con},\ldots,\textup{$k$-con}\}
.
Note that given
\mathcal{P}
and
\mathbf{e}
, the
k
-set
\mathbf{e}
has a unique type with respect to
\mathcal{P}
.
Given multiple collections
\mathcal{P}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{r}
of paths, for
i\in[r]
, we use
\tau(\mathbf{e},i)
to denote the type of
\mathbf{e}
with respect to
\mathcal{P}_{i}
, and for
\tau\in\mathcal{T}
, we set
\mathcal{I}_{\tau}(\mathbf{e})=\{i\in[r]\colon\tau(\mathbf{e},i)=\tau\}
, where we tacitly assume that the index set and the collection of paths that belongs to a given index are obvious from the context.

Proposition 4.1
.

Suppose
1/n\ll\varrho,1/L\ll\eta,\mu,1/k
.
Let
H
be an
\eta
-intersecting
k
-graph on
n
vertices with vertex set
V
such that there is an integer
r
with
kr\leq d_{H}(v)\leq(1+\varrho)kr
for all
v\in V
.
Then, there exist edge-disjoint collections
\mathcal{P}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{r}
of
L
-paths in
H
with
\lvert V(\mathcal{P}_{i})\rvert\geq(1-\mu)n
for all
i\in[r]
such that the following holds for all
\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}
.

(i)

\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\textup{lo}}(\mathbf{e})\rvert\leq\mu r
;

(ii)

\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\textup{$j$-con}}(\mathbf{e})\rvert\leq n^{k-j}/\eta^{2L}
for all
j\in[k-1]
and
\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\textup{$k$-con}}(\mathbf{e})\rvert\leq n/\eta^{2L}
;

(iii)

\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\textup{$j$-end}}(\mathbf{e})\rvert\leq n^{k-j}/L^{1/2}
for all
j\in[k-1]
.

Note that the proof also yields edge-disjoint collections
\mathcal{C}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{r}
of
L
-cycles instead of the paths with
\lvert V(\mathcal{C}_{i})\rvert\geq(1-\mu)n
for all
i\in[r]
(without the properties
(i)
–
(iii)
);
we use this in the proof of Lemma
6.3
.

Proof of Proposition
4.1
.

First we argue that it suffices to find collections
\mathcal{C}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{r}
of
L
-cycles in
H
with properties similar to those of collections of paths in the statement; then we obtain such collections of cycles by applying Corollary
3.6
in an auxiliary hypergraph that represents a fractional cycle decomposition given by Theorem
3.4
.

Suppose
\mathcal{C}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{r}
are edge-disjoint collections of
L
-cycles in
H
.
Note that for all
j\in[k-1]
and
\mathbf{x}\subseteq\binom{V}{j}
, there are at most
n^{k-j}
collections
\mathcal{C}_{i}
with
i\in[r]
where the elements of
\mathbf{x}
appear consecutively in a cycle in
\mathcal{C}_{i}
and for all
i\in[r]
, there is at most one cycle
C\in\mathcal{C}_{i}
such that the elements of
\mathbf{x}
appear consecutively in
C
.
Now, for all
i\in[r]
and every cycle in
C\in\mathcal{C}_{i}
, delete
k-1
consecutive edges uniformly at random and independently of the edges deleted in the other cycles to obtain collections of paths
\mathcal{P}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{P}_{r}
.
Then the expected value of the random variable counting the number of collections
\mathcal{P}_{i}
with
i\in[r]
where
\mathbf{x}
is an end-set of a path in
\mathcal{P}_{i}
is at most
2n^{k-j}/L
.
Hence Chernoff’s inequality (Lemma
3.1
) entails that it is possible to delete
k-1
consecutive edges of every cycle in
\mathcal{C}_{i}
for all
i\in[r]
to obtain collections of paths
\mathcal{P}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{P}_{r}
such that for all
j\in[k-1]
and
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{j}
, there are at most
3n^{k-j}/L
collections
\mathcal{P}_{i}
with
i\in[r]
where
\mathbf{x}
is an end-set of a path in
\mathcal{P}_{i}
.
For such collections
\mathcal{P}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{P}_{r}
,
j\in[k-1]
and
\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}
, we have
\mathcal{I}_{\textup{$j$-end}}(\mathbf{e})\leq\binom{k}{j}\cdot 3n^{k-j}/L\leq n^{k-j}/L^{1/2}
and thus it suffices to obtain edge-disjoint collections
\mathcal{C}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{r}
of
L
-cycles in
H
with
\lvert V(\mathcal{C}_{i})\rvert\geq(1-\mu)n
for all
i\in[r]
such that the following holds.

•

\lvert\{i\in[r]\colon v\notin V(\mathcal{C}_{i})\}\rvert\leq\mu r/k
for all
v\in V
;

•

\lvert\{i\in[r]\colon\exists C\in\mathcal{C}_{i}\colon\mathbf{x}\subseteq V(C)\}\rvert\leq n^{k-j}/(\eta^{2L}\binom{k}{j})
for all
j\in[k-1]
and
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{j}
.

Let
E=E(H)
and let
\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)
denote the set of
L
-cycles in
H
.
From Theorem
3.4
we obtain a fractional
L
-cycle decomposition
\omega
of
H
with

(4.1)

\frac{\lvert E\rvert}{n^{L}}\leq\omega(C)\leq\frac{3\lvert E\rvert}{\eta^{L}n^{L}}

for all
C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)
.
Consider the
2L
-graph
H^{\star}
with vertex set
(V\times[r])\cup E
where we add for each
C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)
and all
i\in[r]
, the edge
e_{C,i}^{\star}=\{(v,i)\colon v\in V(C)\}\cup E(C)
(note that the edge
e_{C,i}^{\star}
uniquely identifies
C
and
i
).
Let
E^{\star}=E(H^{\star})
and
\Gamma=(1+\varrho)r\geq\Delta(H)/k
and let
\omega^{\star}\colon E^{\star}\rightarrow[0,1]
be the edge weight function with
\omega^{\star}(e_{C,i}^{\star})=\omega(C)/\Gamma
for all
e^{\star}\in E^{\star}
. Here,
\omega^{\star}
is a representation of
\omega
that is normalized such that for all
v\in V
and
i\in[r]
, we have

(4.2)

\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e^{\star}\in E^{\star}\colon\\
(v,i)\in e^{\star}\end{subarray}}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})=\frac{1}{k}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e\in E(H)\colon\\
v\in e\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon\\
e\in E(C)\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}=\frac{1}{k}\cdot\frac{d_{H}(v)}{\Gamma}\in\biggl[\frac{1}{1+\varrho},1\biggr].

Note that there is a correspondence of matchings in
H^{\star}
to edge-disjoint collections of
L
-cycles in
H
, namely a matching
\mathcal{M}^{\star}
in
H^{\star}
corresponds to the collections
\mathcal{C}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{r}
, where
\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon e_{C,i}^{\star}\in\mathcal{M}^{\star}\}
for all
i\in[r]
.
This will allow us to obtain collections of cycles with the desired properties from Corollary
3.6
.
We now introduce appropriate parameters including suitable subsets of
E^{\star}
and check that the conditions necessary for a suitable application of Corollary
3.6
hold in this setting.

Let
\delta=\frac{1}{3L}
,
\varepsilon=\frac{\delta}{900L^{2}}
, and
c=n^{L}
.
From (
4.1
) we obtain (with some room to spare)

(4.3)

\frac{1}{c}\leq\frac{\eta}{2k!\Gamma n^{L-k}}\leq\frac{\lvert E\rvert}{\Gamma n^{L}}\leq\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}\leq\frac{3\lvert E\rvert}{\eta^{L}\Gamma n^{L}}\leq\frac{3}{\eta^{L}\Gamma n^{L-k}}\leq\frac{1}{n^{L-3/2}}c^{-\delta}

for all
C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)
. To complete our analysis of the
1
-degrees in
H^{\star}
, we observe that in addition to (
4.2
), for all
e\in E
, we have

(4.4)

\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e^{\star}\in E^{\star}\colon\\
e\in e^{\star}\end{subarray}}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})=r\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon\\
e\in E(C)\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}=r\cdot\frac{1}{\Gamma}\leq 1.

Let us now consider the
2
-degrees in
H^{\star}
.
For distinct
u,v\in V
and distinct
e,f\in E
, we have

\displaystyle\lvert\{C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon u,v\in V(C)\}\rvert\leq Ln^{L-2},\quad\lvert\{C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon v\in V(C)\wedge e\in E(C)\}\rvert\leq k!n^{L-k}

\displaystyle\text{and}\quad\lvert\{C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon e,f\in E(C)\}\rvert\leq 2k!n^{L-k-1}.

Using (
4.3
), this yields for all
i\in[r]
, that

(4.5)

\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e^{\star}\in E^{\star}:\\
(u,i),(v,i)\in e^{\star}\end{subarray}}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H):\\
u,v\in V(C)\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}\leq\frac{L}{n^{1/2}}c^{-\delta}\leq c^{-\delta},

(4.6)

\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e^{\star}\in E^{\star}:\\
(v,i),e\in e^{\star}\end{subarray}}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H):\\
v\in V(C)\wedge e\in E(C)\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}\leq\frac{k!}{n^{k-3/2}}c^{-\delta}\leq c^{-\delta},\quad\text{and}\quad

(4.7)

\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e^{\star}\in E^{\star}:e,f\in e^{\star}\end{subarray}}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})

\displaystyle=r\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H):\\
e,f\in E(C)\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}\leq\frac{2k!r}{n^{k-1/2}}c^{-\delta}\leq c^{-\delta}.

Furthermore, observe that

(4.8)

\sum_{e^{\star}\in E(H^{\star})}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})=r\cdot\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}=r\cdot\frac{\lvert E\rvert}{\Gamma L}\leq\exp(c^{\varepsilon^{2}})

gives an upper bound for the total weight on the edges of
H^{\star}
.
For
i\in[r]
,
v\in V
,
j\in[k-1]
, and
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{j}
, we define edge-sets as follows.

\displaystyle E_{i}^{\star}=\{e_{C,i^{\prime}}^{\star}\in E^{\star}:i^{\prime}=i\},\quad E_{v}^{\star}=\{e_{C,i^{\prime}}^{\star}\in E^{\star}:v\in V(C)\}\quad\text{and}\quad E_{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}=\{e_{C,i^{\prime}}^{\star}\in E^{\star}:\mathbf{x}\subseteq V(C)\}.

We have

(4.9)

\sum_{e^{\star}\in E_{i}^{\star}}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})=\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}=\frac{\lvert E\rvert}{\Gamma L}\geq\frac{rn}{\Gamma L}\geq c^{\delta}

and

(4.10)

\sum_{e^{\star}\in E_{v}^{\star}}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})=r\cdot\frac{1}{k}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e\in E(H)\colon\\
v\in e\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon\\
e\in E(C)\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}=r\cdot\frac{1}{k}\cdot\frac{d_{H}(v)}{\Gamma}\geq\frac{r}{1+\varrho}\geq c^{\delta}.

Since Lemma
3.11
implies
\lvert\{C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon d_{C}(\mathbf{x})\geq 1\}\rvert\geq n^{L-j-1/3}
, using (
4.3
) we obtain

(4.11)

\sum_{e^{\star}\in E_{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})\geq r\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon\\
d_{C}(\mathbf{x})\geq 1\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}\geq r\cdot n^{L-j-1/3}\cdot\frac{\eta}{2k!\Gamma n^{L-k}}\geq n^{k-j-1/2}\geq c^{\delta}.

Thus, since
r+n+\sum_{j\in[k-1]}\binom{n}{j}\leq\exp(c^{\varepsilon^{2}})
holds and by (
4.2
)–(
4.11
) we may apply Corollary
3.6
to obtain a matching
\mathcal{M}^{\star}
in
H^{\star}
with

\lvert\mathcal{M}^{\star}\cap E_{i}^{\star}\rvert\geq(1-c^{-\varepsilon})\frac{\lvert E\rvert}{\Gamma L}\geq(1-c^{-\varepsilon})\frac{rn}{\Gamma L}\geq(1-\mu)\frac{n}{L},

\lvert\mathcal{M}^{\star}\cap E_{v}^{\star}\rvert\geq(1-c^{-\varepsilon})\frac{r}{k}\cdot\frac{d_{H}(v)}{\Gamma}\geq(1-c^{-\varepsilon})\frac{r^{2}}{\Gamma}\geq\biggl(1-\frac{\mu}{k}\biggr)r,

and

\lvert\mathcal{M}^{\star}\cap E_{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}\rvert\leq(1+c^{-\varepsilon})\sum_{e^{\star}\in E_{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}}\omega^{\star}(e^{\star})

for all
i\in[r]
,
v\in V
,
j\in[k-1]
, and
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{j}
. Since we have
\lvert\{C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon\mathbf{x}\subseteq V(C)\}\rvert\leq L^{j}n^{L-j}
, (
4.3
) implies

\lvert\mathcal{M}^{\star}\cap E_{\mathbf{x}}^{\star}\rvert\leq(1+c^{-\varepsilon})r\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in\mathcal{C}_{L}(H)\colon\\
\mathbf{x}\subseteq V(C)\end{subarray}}\frac{\omega(C)}{\Gamma}\leq(1+c^{-\varepsilon})r\cdot L^{j}n^{L-j}\cdot\frac{3}{\eta^{L}\Gamma n^{L-k}}\leq\frac{1}{\eta^{2L}\binom{k}{j}}n^{k-j}

and thus, choosing
\mathcal{C}_{i}
as the collection of
L
-cycles
C
in
H
with
e_{C,i}^{\star}\in\mathcal{M}^{\star}
yields collections of cycles in
H
with the desired properties.
∎

5.
Ingredients for absorption

Suppose we are given a
k
-graph
H
on
n
vertices.
In this section we construct a collection of paths
\mathcal{P}
in
H
whose lengths do not grow with
n

such that any small set of vertices
X
can be absorbed into these paths; that is, for every path
P\in\mathcal{P}
, there is a new path
P^{\prime}
with the same end-tuples as
P
and
V(P^{\prime})\subseteq V(P)\cup X
such that the new paths form a collection of paths
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
with
V(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})=V(P)\cup X
.

There are two main novelties in our setting.
Firstly, we choose
\mathcal{P}
randomly in an extremely uniform way such that
V(\mathcal{P})
behaves like a uniformly chosen vertex set of size
|V(\mathcal{P})|
.
Secondly, we can control how many vertices each path in
\mathcal{P}
will absorb if an adversary determines a set of vertices to absorb.
Here the main difficulty is that the lengths of the paths in
\mathcal{P}
do not grow with
n
.
To the best of our knowledge, this problem has not been dealt with in the literature so far.

5.1.
Random walks and vertex absorbers

Let
H
be a
k
-graph on
n
vertices with vertex set
V
and edge set
E
.
For
x\in V
, a path
A=a_{1}\ldots a_{2k}
in
H
is called an
x
-absorber
1
1

1

The reader familiar with the topic knows that usually absorbers consist of
2k-2
vertices; in fact, we only deviate from this to enhance readability and simplify some arguments.
if
a_{1}\ldots a_{k}xa_{k+1}\ldots a_{2k}
is also a path in
H
.
In what follows, we describe how certain random walks contain many vertex-disjoint
x
-absorbers for all
x\in V
simultaneously
and at the same time ensure that the set of vertices visited by these random walks behaves like a vertex set chosen uniformly at random among all vertex sets of the same size.

In what follows,
a
,
i
,
\ell
,
L
,
t_{\star}
are always positive integers.
Let
W=w_{1}\ldots w_{L}
be a walk.
For
i\in[L/(2k+\ell)]
, we define

A^{\ell}_{i}(W)=w_{(2k+\ell)(i-1)+1}\ldots w_{(2k+\ell)(i-1)+2k}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(W)=\biggl\{A^{\ell}_{i}(W)\colon i\in\biggl[\frac{L}{2k+\ell}\biggr]\biggr\}.

We may think of
A^{\ell}_{i}
as the
i
-th potential absorber in
W
when requiring
\ell
vertices between absorbers whereas
\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(W)
is the set of all these potential absorbers in
W
.
To gain control over where absorbed vertices will be placed, we consider absorbers in groups which we call
blocks
.
Towards the end of the section, our construction yields a set of blocks
\mathcal{B}
and during the absorption, every block
B\in\mathcal{B}
will absorb exactly one vertex.
More precisely, we say that a walk
B=b_{1}\ldots b_{a(2k+\ell)}
in
H
is an
(a,\ell)
-block
in
H
; that is,
B
can be split into
a
consecutive walks that consist of a
2k
-walk followed by an
\ell
-walk.
For
i\in[L/(a(2k+\ell))]
, we define

B^{a,\ell}_{i}(W)=w_{a(2k+\ell)(i-1)+1}\ldots w_{a(2k+\ell)i}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{B}^{a,\ell}(W)=\biggl\{B^{a,\ell}_{i}(W)\colon i\in\biggl[\frac{L}{a(2k+\ell)}\biggr]\biggr\}

where
B^{a,\ell}_{i}(W)
can be considered as the
i
-th
(a,\ell)
-block in
W
whereas
\mathcal{B}^{a,\ell}(W)
is the set of all these
(a,\ell)
-blocks in
W
.
Later, we will choose absorbers and blocks randomly.
In contrast to other approaches existing in the literature,
we build our absorbing structure via random walks whose distributions are given by perfect fractional matchings to ensure a very uniform distribution of the vertices visited by these random walks.

We introduce the convention that sequences
s_{m}\ldots s_{n}
with
m>n
are considered as the empty sequence which we identify with
\varnothing
.
For
\omega\colon E\rightarrow{\mathds{R}}_{\geq 0}
,
j\in[k]
, and
v_{1},\ldots,v_{j}\in V
,
we define
\omega(v_{1}\ldots v_{j})=\sum_{e\in E\colon v_{1},\ldots,v_{j}\in e}\omega(e)
and we set
\omega(\varnothing)=\sum_{e\in E}\omega(e)
.

Let
\omega\colon E\rightarrow{\mathds{R}}_{>0}
.
We say a sequence of
V
-valued random variables
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
is a random walk in
H

with parameters
(L,\omega)
, or simply an
(L,\omega)
-random walk
in
H
, if its distribution is given by

(5.1)

\displaystyle\mathds{P}[X_{t}=v_{t}\mid X_{1}\ldots X_{t-1}=v_{1}\ldots v_{t-1}]

\displaystyle=\mathds{P}[X_{t}=v_{t}\mid X_{t-m}\ldots X_{t-1}=v_{t-m}\ldots v_{t-1}]

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{\omega(v_{t-m}\ldots v_{t})}{(k-m)\omega(v_{t-m}\ldots v_{t-1})}&\text{if\penalty\ $v_{t}\notin\{v_{t-m},\ldots,v_{t-1}\}$}\\
0&\text{if\penalty\ $v_{t}\in\{v_{t-m},\ldots,v_{t-1}\}$}\end{cases}

for all
t\in[t_{\star}]
,
m=\min\{k-1,t-1\mod L\}
, and
v_{1},\ldots,v_{t}\in V
with
\mathds{P}[X_{1}\ldots X_{t-1}=v_{1}\ldots v_{t-1}]>0
. This is indeed a probability distribution because for all
j\in[k-1]
and
v_{1},\ldots,v_{j}\in V
, we have

\sum_{v\in V\smallsetminus\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{j}\}}\omega(v_{1}\ldots v_{j}v)=(k-j)\omega(v_{1}\ldots v_{j}).

Whenever we consider an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in a
k
-graph
H
, we assume that
L
is a positive integer and
\omega\colon E(H)\rightarrow{\mathds{R}}_{>0}
.
Observe that if
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
is an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in a
k
-graph
H
, then also
X_{L(s-1)+1}\ldots X_{Ls}
is an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in
H
for all
s\in[t_{\star}/L]
.

Observation 5.1
.

Suppose
H
is a
k
-graph.
Suppose
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
is an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in
H
.
Then, the random walks
X_{1}\ldots X_{Ls}
and
X_{Ls+1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
are independent for all positive integers
s
.

Recall that
\omega\colon E\rightarrow{\mathds{R}}_{>0}
is
balanced
if
\frac{\max_{e\in E}\omega(e)}{\min_{e\in E}\omega(e)}\leq 2
.
For an
(L,\omega)
-random walk
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
in
H
for some balanced
\omega
, the balancedness of
\omega
allows us to bound the probability of the event that
X_{t}=X_{t^{\prime}}
for some distinct
t,t^{\prime}\in[t_{\star}]
; the union bound yields the following observation.

Observation 5.2
.

Let
1/n\ll\eta,1/k
.
Suppose
H
is a
k
-graph on
n
vertices with
\delta(H)\geq\eta n
.
Suppose
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
with
t_{\star}\leq 2n^{1/3}
is an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in
H
for some balanced
\omega
.
Then, we have

\mathds{P}[\text{$X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}$ is self-avoiding}]\geq 1-n^{-1/4}.

The following lemma shows that
for an
(L,\omega)
-random walk
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
in
H
not only the transition probabilities are determined by
\omega
,
but also the probability of
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
consecutively visiting a sequence of vertices can be easily computed in terms of
\omega
.

Lemma 5.3
.

Suppose
H
is a
k
-graph on
n
vertices with vertex set
V
.
Suppose
X_{1}\ldots X_{L}
is an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in
H
.
Let
t\in[L]
and
j\in[\min\{k,t\}]
. Then, we have

(5.2)

\mathds{P}[X_{t-j+1}\ldots X_{t}=v_{-j+1}\ldots v_{0}]=\frac{(k-j)!\omega(v_{-j+1}\ldots v_{0})}{k!\omega(\varnothing)}

for all
v_{-j+1},\ldots,v_{0}\in V
.

Proof.

We prove the statement by induction on
t
.
If
t=1
, then the statement is true by choice of
X_{1}
.
Next assume that (
5.2
) is true for a
t\in[L-1]
and all
j\in[\min\{k,t\}]
.

Given such a
t\in[L-1]
, let
j\in[\min\{k,t+1\}]
and
m=\min\{k-1,t\}
(hence
j\leq m+1
) as well as
v_{-j+1},\ldots,v_{0}\in V
be given. Furthermore, let
U=V\smallsetminus\{v_{-j+1},\ldots,v_{0}\}
and
h=m-j+1\geq 0
.
Now we establish (
5.2
) with
t+1
instead of
t
. We compute

\displaystyle\mathds{P}[X_{t-j+2}\ldots X_{t+1}=v_{-j+1}\ldots v_{0}]

\displaystyle=\sum_{(v_{-m},\ldots,v_{-j})\in{U}^{\underline{h}}}\mathds{P}[X_{t-m+1}\ldots X_{t+1}=v_{-m}\ldots v_{0}]

(5.3)

\displaystyle=\sum_{(v_{-m},\ldots,v_{-j})\in{U}^{\underline{h}}}\frac{\omega(v_{-m}\ldots v_{0})\mathds{P}[X_{t-m+1}\ldots X_{t}=v_{-m}\ldots v_{-1}]}{(k-m)\omega(v_{-m}\ldots v_{-1})}

(5.4)

\displaystyle=\sum_{(v_{-m},\ldots,v_{-j})\in{U}^{\underline{h}}}\frac{\omega(v_{-m}\ldots v_{0})\cdot(k-m)!\omega(v_{-m}\ldots v_{-1})}{(k-m)\omega(v_{-m}\ldots v_{-1})\cdot k!\omega(\varnothing)}

\displaystyle=\frac{(k-m-1)!}{k!\omega(\varnothing)}\sum_{(v_{-m},\ldots,v_{-j})\in{U}^{\underline{h}}}\omega(v_{-m}\ldots v_{0})

\displaystyle=\frac{(k-m-1)!}{k!\omega(\varnothing)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e\in E\colon\\
v_{-j+1},\ldots,v_{0}\in e\end{subarray}}\binom{k-j}{h}\cdot h!\cdot\omega(e)

\displaystyle=\frac{(k-j)!\omega(v_{-j+1}\ldots v_{0})}{k!\omega(\varnothing)},

where we used (
5.1
) for (
5.3
) and the induction hypothesis for (
5.4
).
∎

The next lemma shows that whenever
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
is an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in
H
for some balanced
\omega
and
x
a vertex in a slightly larger
k
-graph, then after a few steps
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
has a decent chance of producing an
x
-absorber in
2k
consecutive steps.
This follows easily, because as an
\eta
-intersecting
k
-graph,
H
contains sufficiently many suitable
x
-absorbers, Lemma
3.11
guarantees that there are sufficiently many ways for the random walk to arrive at such an
x
-absorber independent of the starting conditions and the balancedness of
\omega
entails that every walk extending an already chosen initial segment of the random walk occurs with sufficiently large probability.

Observation 5.4
.

Let
1/n\ll\alpha\ll\nu_{+},\ell\ll\eta,1/k
and
L\geq 2k
.
Suppose
H_{+}
is an
\eta
-intersecting
k
-graph on at most
(1+\nu_{+})n
vertices with vertex set
V_{+}
and
H
is an induced subgraph of
H_{+}
on
n
vertices.
Suppose
X_{1}\ldots X_{L}
is an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in
H
for some balanced
\omega
. Then, for all
t\in\{-\ell,\ldots,L-\ell-2k\}
and
x\in V_{+}
, we have

\mathds{P}[\text{$X_{t+\ell+1}\ldots X_{t+\ell+2k}$ is an\penalty\ $x$-absorber in\penalty\ $H_{+}$}\mid X_{1}\ldots X_{t}]\geq\alpha.

Measuring the impact of removing the vertices of an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in
H
from
H
is one of the core objectives in this subsection.
The following lemma shows that for each
(k-1)
-set of vertices of
H
, its neighbourhood is essentially visited as often as expected.
Via Lemma
3.10
, this transfers to the vertex degrees appropriately.

Lemma 5.5
.

Let
1/n\ll\eta,1/k,1/L
.
Suppose
H
is a
k
-graph on
n
vertices with vertex set
V
and
\delta(H)\geq\eta n
.
Suppose
X_{1}\ldots X_{t_{\star}}
with
n^{1/3}/2\leq t_{\star}\leq 2n^{1/3}
is an
(L,\omega)
-random walk in
H
for some balanced perfect fractional matching
\omega
in
H
. Let
U=V\smallsetminus\{X_{t}\colon t\in[t_{\star}]\}
.
Then, for all
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
, we have

(5.5)

\mathds{P}\biggl[d_{H[U\cup\mathbf{x}]}(\mathbf{x})=(1\pm n^{-31/40})\biggl(1-\frac{t_{\star}}{n}\biggr)d_{H}(\mathbf{x})\biggr]\geq 1-\exp(-n^{1/14}).

Proof.

Since Lemma
5.3
yields
\mathds{P}[X_{t}=v]=1/n
for all
t\in[t_{\star}]
and
v\in V
and since for all
\ell\in[L]
, the random variables
X_{L(s-1)+\ell}
with
s\in[t_{\star}/L]
are mutually independent by Observation
5.1
, the statement is a consequence of Chernoff’s inequality (Lemma
3.1
).

Let us turn to the details.
Fix
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
.
To see that (
5.5
) holds, we will show that

(5.6)

\mathds{P}\biggl[\lvert N_{H}(\mathbf{x})\cap\{X_{t}\colon t\in[t_{\star}]\}\rvert=(1\pm n^{-1/8})\frac{t_{\star}}{n}\lvert N_{H}(\mathbf{x})\rvert\biggr]\geq 1-\exp(-n^{1/14}).

To this end, for
t\in[L]
, let
Y_{t}
denote the indicator random variable of the event that
X_{t}\in N_{H}(\mathbf{x})
.
Note that Lemma
5.3
implies
\mathds{P}[Y_{t}=1]=\lvert N_{H}(\mathbf{x})\rvert/n
.
For
\ell\in[L]
, let
N_{\ell}=\sum_{s\in[t_{\star}/L]}Y_{L(s-1)+\ell}
.
Crucially, note that
N_{\ell}
is the sum of the independent random variables
Y_{L(s-1)+\ell}
with
s\in[t_{\star}/L]
.
Furthermore, for
t\in[t_{\star}]
, let
Z_{t}
denote the indicator random variable of the event that
X_{t}\in\{X_{t^{\prime}}\colon t^{\prime}\in[t-1]\}\cap N_{H}(\mathbf{x})
and let
Z=\sum_{t\in[t_{\star}]}Z_{t}
.
Observe that

\lvert N_{H}(\mathbf{x})\cap\{X_{t}\colon t\in[t_{\star}]\}\rvert=\sum_{\ell\in[L]}N_{\ell}-Z.

Let us estimate
N_{\ell}
and
Z
.
For all
\ell\in[L]
, Chernoff’s inequality (Lemma
3.1
) entails

\mathds{P}\biggl[N_{\ell}=\biggl(1\pm\frac{n^{-1/8}}{2}\biggr)\frac{\lvert N_{H}(\mathbf{x})\rvert}{n}\frac{t_{\star}}{L}\biggr]\geq 1-\exp(-n^{1/13}).

Furthermore, from
t_{\star}\leq 2n^{1/3}
,
\delta(H)\geq\eta n
, (
5.1
), and the balancedness of
\omega
, we obtain

\mathds{P}[Z_{t}=1\mid Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{t-1}]\leq n^{-1/2}

for all
t\in[t_{\star}]
. This shows that
Z
is stochastically dominated by a binomial random variable with parameters
t_{\star}
and
n^{-1/2}
and thus Chernoff’s inequality (Lemma
3.1
) implies

\displaystyle\mathds{P}\biggl[Z\geq\frac{n^{-1/8}}{2}\frac{t_{\star}}{n}\lvert N_{H}(\mathbf{x})\rvert\biggr]

\displaystyle\leq\mathds{P}\biggl[Z\geq\biggl(1+\frac{\eta}{3}n^{3/8}\biggr)n^{-1/2}t_{\star}\biggr]

\displaystyle\leq\exp(-n^{1/6}).

The union bound yields (
5.6
).
∎

5.2.
Building the absorbing structure

The following result verifies the existence of few vertex-disjoint paths whose union contains many vertex absorbers.
Moreover, there is in fact a “uniform” probabilistic construction of these paths.
To state the next result, we introduce the following terminology concerning paths.
For a path
P=v_{1}\ldots v_{\ell}
, we define the boundary
\partial P
as
\partial P=P[\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k},v_{\ell-k+1},\ldots,v_{\ell}\}]
if
\ell\geq 2k+1
and
\partial P=P
otherwise.
Furthermore, for a collection of paths
\mathcal{P}
, we define
\partial\mathcal{P}=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\partial P
.

Lemma 5.6
.

Let
1/n\ll\varrho\ll 1/L\ll 1/a\ll\nu_{+},1/\ell\ll\eta,1/k
.
Suppose
H_{+}
is an
\eta
-intersecting
k
-graph on at most
(1+\nu_{+})n
vertices with vertex set
V_{+}
and
H
is an induced
\varrho
-almost regular subgraph of
H_{+}
on
n
vertices with edge set
E
.
Let
\vartheta=1/a
and for all
x\in V_{+}
, denote the set of
x
-absorbers in
H_{+}
by
\mathcal{A}_{x}
.
Then, there is a probabilistic construction of a collection
\mathcal{P}
of
L
-paths in
H
together with a set
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathcal{B}^{a,\ell}(P)
such that the following holds.

(i)

\lvert\mathcal{P}\rvert\leq\vartheta^{2}n/L
;

(ii)

H-V(\mathcal{P})
is
2\varrho
-almost regular;

(iii)

\lvert\{B\in\mathcal{B}\colon\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)\cap\mathcal{A}_{x}\neq\varnothing\}\rvert\geq 3\vartheta^{4}n
for all
x\in V_{+}
(in particular,
\lvert\mathcal{B}\rvert\geq 3\vartheta^{4}n
);

(iv)

\lvert\{x\in V_{+}\colon\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)\cap\mathcal{A}_{x}=\varnothing\}\rvert\leq\vartheta^{4}n
for all
B\in\mathcal{B}
;

(v)

\mathds{P}[e\in E(\mathcal{P})]\leq\vartheta\frac{1}{n^{k-1}}
and
\mathds{P}[e\in E(\partial P)]\leq\frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{n^{k-1}}
for all
e\in E
.

Proof.

The key idea of the proof is as follows. Constructing
\mathcal{P}
by starting with
\mathcal{P}=\varnothing
and iteratively adding suitable random walks in
H
to
\mathcal{P}
yields a
\mathcal{P}
as desired apart from
(v)
with probability at least
1/5
. This can be used to obtain an appropriate probability distribution on such collections
\mathcal{P}
.

More precisely, for
t_{\star}=n^{1/3}
, we will construct
\mathcal{P}
in
s_{\star}=\vartheta^{2}n/t_{\star}

stages
, where in stage
s\in[s_{\star}]
we potentially add the
L
-walks generated by an
(L,\omega^{s-1})
-random walk
X^{s}=X^{s}_{1}\ldots X^{s}_{t_{\star}}
in a random subgraph
H^{s-1}
of
H
for a balanced perfect fractional matching
\omega^{s-1}
in
H^{s-1}
.
To this end, for every subgraph
S\subseteq H
with a balanced perfect fractional matching, fix one such perfect fractional matching in
S
to which we refer as the perfect fractional matching
assigned
to
S
.
We inductively define the random
k
-graphs
H=H^{0}\supseteq\ldots\supseteq H^{s_{\star}}
and random walks
X^{1},\ldots,X^{s_{\star}}
as follows.

(1)

Let
H^{0}=H
;

(2)

for
s\in[s_{\star}]
, define the random walk
X^{s}=X^{s}_{1}\ldots X^{s}_{t_{\star}}
in
H^{s-1}
and
H^{s}\subseteq H^{s-1}
as follows.

(2a)

If there is a balanced perfect fractional matching in
H^{s-1}
, let
X^{s}=X^{s}_{1}\ldots X^{s}_{t_{\star}}
be an
(L,\omega^{s-1})
-random walk in
H^{s-1}
, where
\omega^{s-1}
denotes the perfect fractional matching assigned to
H^{s-1}
;
otherwise let
X^{s}=X^{s-1}
;

(2b)

if
X^{s}
is self-avoiding, let
H^{s}=H^{s-1}-\{X^{s}_{t}\colon t\in[t_{\star}]\}
;
otherwise let
H^{s}=H^{s-1}
.

Note that Lemma
3.8
guarantees a balanced perfect fractional matching in
H_{0}=H
and that for
s\in[s_{\star}]
, if
X^{s}=X^{s-1}
, then
H^{s}=H^{s-1}
by construction of
H^{s-1}
even if
X^{s}
is self-avoiding.

We may think of stages
s\in[s_{\star}]
where there is no balanced perfect fractional matching in
H^{s-1}
and stages
s\in[s_{\star}]
where
X^{s}
is not self-avoiding as
failed
stages as these stages fail to generate
L
-paths disjoint from each other and all
L
-paths previously added to
\mathcal{P}
. While stages that fail due to the absence of a balanced perfect fractional matching in
H^{s-1}
are
fatal
in the sense that they entail failure in all subsequent stages, we can otherwise recover from failure in the sense that subsequent stages may still be successful. We repeat previously generated paths in the case of fatal failure simply for convenience.

Later we show that with probability at least
4/5
no fatal failure occurs; that is, there is a balanced perfect fractional matching in
H^{s-1}
for all
s\in[s_{\star}]
. We also show that with probability at least
4/5
, there are at most
n^{1/2}
non-fatal failures, that is, there are at most
n^{1/2}
stages
s\in[s_{\star}]
such that
X^{s}
is not self-avoiding.

For
s\in[s_{\star}]_{0}
, let
V^{s}=V(H^{s})
and let
V=V^{0}=V(H)
.
We use
p_{\star}=t_{\star}/L
to refer to the number of
L
-walks generated in every stage. For
s\in[s_{\star}]
and
p\in[p_{\star}]
, let
P^{s}_{p}=X^{s}_{L(p-1)+1}\ldots X^{s}_{Lp}
denote the
p
-th walk generated in stage
s
and let
\mathcal{P}^{s}=\{P^{s}_{p}\colon p\in[p_{\star}]\}
denote the set of all walks generated in stage
s
. Let

\displaystyle\mathcal{P}^{\prime}=\bigcup_{s\in[s_{\star}]}\mathcal{P}^{s},\qquad\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime}}\mathcal{B}^{a,\ell}(P),

\displaystyle\mathcal{P}=\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in[s_{\star}]\colon\text{$X^{s}$ is self-avoiding}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{P}^{s}\qquad\text{ and}\qquad\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P})=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathcal{B}^{a,\ell}(P).

In accordance with
(iv)
, we say that an
(a,\ell)
-block
B
is
good
if there are at most
\vartheta^{4}n
vertices
x\in V_{+}
such that
\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)
does not contain an
x
-absorber in
H_{+}
and we call
B

bad
otherwise.
We define events
\mathcal{E}_{1}
,
\mathcal{E}_{2}
,
\mathcal{E}_{3}
, and
\mathcal{E}_{4}
as follows.

\mathcal{E}_{1}
:

For all
x\in V_{+}
, there are at least
5\vartheta^{4}n
triples
(s,p,i)
with
s\in[s_{\star}]
,
p\in[p_{\star}]
,
i\in[L/(a(2k+\ell))]
, and
\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B^{a,\ell}_{i}(P^{s}_{p}))\cap\mathcal{A}_{x}\neq\varnothing
;

\mathcal{E}_{2}
:

there are at most
\vartheta^{4}n
bad blocks in
\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})
;

\mathcal{E}_{3}
:

there are at most
n^{1/2}
stages
s\in[s_{\star}]
such that
X^{s}
is not self-avoiding;

\mathcal{E}_{4}
:

H^{s_{\star}}
is
(\varrho+n^{-1/12})
-almost regular.

We claim the following.

(5.7)

If
\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_{1}\cap\ldots\cap\mathcal{E}_{4}
occurs, then
\mathcal{P}
with
\mathcal{B}=\{B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P})\colon\text{$B$ is good}\}
satisfies
(i)
–
(iv)
.

To see that this is true, we argue as follows.
First observe that since
H-X
is
(\eta/2)
-intersecting for all
X\subseteq V
of size at most
\eta n/2
, the random
k
-graphs
H^{s}
with
s\in[s_{\star}]
are
(\eta/2)
-intersecting. Thus if
\mathcal{E}_{4}
occurs, there exists a balanced perfect fractional matching in
H^{s_{\star}}
by Lemma
3.8
. This implies that there was a balanced perfect fractional matching in
H^{s}
for all
s\in[s_{\star}]_{0}
and thus no fatal failure occured; otherwise
H^{s_{\star}}
would be equal to the first such
k
-graph without a perfect fractional matching by construction.

Next note that if
\mathcal{E}_{1}\cap\mathcal{E}_{3}
occurs, the number of triples
(s,p,i)
with
s\in[s_{\star}]
,
p\in[p_{\star}]
,
i\in[L/(a(2k+\ell))]
, and
\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B^{a,\ell}_{i}(P^{s}_{p}))\cap\mathcal{A}_{x}\neq\varnothing
such that
X^{s}
is self-avoiding is at least
4\vartheta^{4}n
for all
x\in V_{+}
. This together with the previous observation shows that whenever
\mathcal{E}_{1}\cap\mathcal{E}_{3}\cap\mathcal{E}_{4}
occurs we have that for all
x\in V_{+}
, there are at least
4\vartheta^{4}n
blocks
B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P})
with
\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)\cap\mathcal{A}_{x}\neq\varnothing
. If
\mathcal{E}_{2}
now also occurs in addition to
\mathcal{E}_{1}\cap\mathcal{E}_{3}\cap\mathcal{E}_{4}
, we lose at most
\vartheta^{4}n
blocks by dropping bad blocks which shows that
(iii)
holds.

Finally, since we only consider good blocks,
(iv)
holds,
s_{\star}\cdot p_{\star}=\vartheta^{2}n/L
implies that
(i)
holds by construction of
\mathcal{P}
, and if
\mathcal{E}_{4}
occurs,
(ii)
holds because
H-V(\mathcal{P})=H^{s_{\star}}
.
This proves (
5.7
).

Let us finish the proof assuming
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{E}]\geq 1/5
. By (
5.7
), this implies that choosing
\hat{\mathcal{P}}
from all possible realisations of
\mathcal{P}
such that
\mathds{P}[\hat{\mathcal{P}}=\mathcal{Q}]=\mathds{P}[\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{Q}\mid\mathcal{E}]
for all possible realisations
\mathcal{Q}
of
\mathcal{P}
is a probabilistic construction as desired because for all
e\in E
and
i\in[L-k+1]
, Lemma
5.3
entails

\displaystyle\mathds{P}[\exists(X_{t})_{t\in[L]}\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}\colon\{X_{i},\ldots,X_{i+k-1}\}=e]

\displaystyle=\mathds{P}[\exists(X_{t})_{t\in[L]}\in\mathcal{P}\colon\{X_{i},\ldots,X_{i+k-1}\}=e\mid\mathcal{E}]

\displaystyle\leq 5\sum_{s\in[s_{\star}]}\sum_{(X_{t})_{t\in[L]}\in\mathcal{P}^{s}}\mathds{P}[\{X_{i},\ldots,X_{i+k-1}\}=e]

\displaystyle=5\sum_{s\in[s_{\star}]}\sum_{(X_{t})_{t\in[L]}\in\mathcal{P}^{s}}k!\frac{\omega^{s-1}(e)}{k!\omega^{s-1}(\varnothing)}

\displaystyle\leq 5\cdot s_{\star}\cdot p_{\star}\cdot k!\cdot 2\frac{1}{\frac{\eta}{2}n^{k}}\leq\frac{\vartheta}{L}\frac{1}{n^{k-1}},

which implies
(v)
.

It remains to prove
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{E}]\geq 1/5
. This easily follows if
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{E}_{i}]\geq 4/5
for all
i\in[4]
, which is what we prove next. For
x\in V_{+}
and
s\in[s_{\star}]
, let
Y_{x,s}
denote the random variable counting the pairs
(p,i)
with
p\in[p_{\star}]
,
i\in[L/(2k+\ell)]
, and
A^{\ell}_{i}(P^{s}_{p})\in\mathcal{A}_{x}
. Note that
\mathcal{E}_{1}
occurs if
Y_{x,s}\geq 5\vartheta^{3}n/s_{\star}
for all
x\in V_{+}
and
s\in[s_{\star}]
.
Observation
5.1
in conjunction with Observation
5.4
shows that
Y_{x,s}
stochastically dominates a binomial random variable with parameters
p_{\star}\frac{L}{2k+\ell}
and
\vartheta^{1/2}
. Hence Chernoff’s inequality (Lemma
3.1
) implies that

\displaystyle\mathds{P}\biggl[Y_{x,s}<\frac{5\vartheta^{3}n}{s_{\star}}\biggr]\leq\mathds{P}\biggl[Y_{x,s}\leq\frac{1}{2}\cdot\vartheta^{1/2}\cdot p_{\star}\frac{L}{2k+\ell}\biggr]\leq\exp(-n^{1/4})

and the union bound yields
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{E}_{1}]\geq 4/5
.

For all
x\in V_{+}
and
B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})
, Observation
5.4
implies

\mathds{P}[\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)\cap\mathcal{A}_{x}=\varnothing]\leq(1-\vartheta^{1/2})^{a}\leq\vartheta^{5}/2.

This entails

\mathds{E}[\lvert\{x\in V_{+}\colon\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)\cap\mathcal{A}_{x}=\varnothing\}\rvert]\leq\vartheta^{5}n.

Using Markov’s inequality we obtain
\mathds{P}[\text{$B$ is bad}]\leq\vartheta
for all
B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})
. This shows that the expected value of the random variable counting the number of bad blocks in
\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})
is at most

\vartheta\cdot s_{\star}\cdot p_{\star}\cdot\frac{L}{a(2k+\ell)}=\frac{\vartheta^{4}}{2k+\ell}n\leq\vartheta^{4}n/5.

Again using Markov’s inequality, this yields
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{E}_{2}]\geq 4/5
.

For all
s\in[s_{\star}]
, Observation
5.2
implies that
X^{s}
is self-avoiding with probability at least
1-2n^{-1/4}
. From this, we obtain that the expected value of the random variable counting the stages
s\in[s_{\star}]
where
X^{s}
is not self-avoiding is at most
2n^{-1/4}\cdot s_{\star}=2\vartheta^{2}n^{5/12}\leq n^{1/2}/5
. Using Markov’s inequality we conclude that
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{E}_{3}]\geq 4/5
.

To see that
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{E}_{4}]\geq 4/5
holds, we show that all random
k
-graphs
H^{s}
with
s\in[s_{\star}]_{0}
are almost regular with high probability.
More precisely, for
s\in[s_{\star}]_{0}
, let
\mathcal{E}^{s}_{4}
denote the event that
H^{s}
is
(\varrho+sn^{-3/4})
-almost regular. Our goal is to show

(5.8)

\mathds{P}\Bigl[\bigcap_{s^{\prime}=0}^{s}\mathcal{E}^{s^{\prime}}_{4}\Bigr]\geq 1-s\exp(n^{-1/15})

for all
s\in[s_{\star}]_{0}
. This suffices because
\mathcal{E}^{s_{\star}}_{4}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{4}
. We proceed by induction on
s
. First note that
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{E}^{0}_{4}]=1
.
Next, assume that (
5.8
) holds for some
s\in[s_{\star}-1]_{0}
.
Then, Lemma
3.8
guarantees that there is no fatal failure in stage
s+1
.
For
U=V^{s}\smallsetminus\{X^{s+1}_{t}\colon t\in[t_{\star}]\}
and
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V^{s}}{k-1}
, Lemma
5.5
entails

\mathds{P}\biggl[d_{H^{s}[U\cup\mathbf{x}]}(\mathbf{x})=(1\pm n^{-31/40})\biggl(1-\frac{t_{\star}}{\lvert V^{s}\rvert}\biggr)d_{H^{s}}(\mathbf{x})\biggm|\bigcap_{s^{\prime}=0}^{s}\mathcal{E}^{s^{\prime}}_{4}\biggr]\geq 1-\exp(-n^{1/14}).

Lemma
3.10
and the union bound yield
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{E}^{s+1}_{4}\mid\bigcap_{s^{\prime}=0}^{s}\mathcal{E}^{s^{\prime}}_{4}]\geq 1-\exp(-n^{1/15})
and thus by induction hypothesis
\mathds{P}[\bigcap_{s^{\prime}=0}^{s+1}\mathcal{E}^{s^{\prime}}_{4}]\geq 1-(s+1)\exp(-n^{1/15})
.
∎

In the following Proposition
5.8
we employ the absorbers provided by Lemma
5.6
to absorb sets of vertices
X
in the sense that for all suitable
X
, we find a selection of these absorbers such that the selected absorbers can simultaneously absorb all vertices in
X
.
As this requires matching all vertices
x\in X
to an
x
-absorber, we make use of the following observation which follows easily by iteratively using Hall’s theorem and removing perfect matchings.

Observation 5.7
.

Suppose
G
is a bipartite graph on
2n
vertices with bipartition
\{V_{1},V_{2}\}
with
\lvert V_{1}\rvert=\lvert V_{2}\rvert=n
.
For
i\in[2]
, let
\delta_{i}=\min\{d_{G}(v)\colon v\in V_{i}¸\}
.
Then, there are at least
(\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}-n)/2
disjoint perfect matchings in
G
.

Proposition 5.8
.

Let
1/n\ll\varrho\ll 1/L\ll\vartheta\ll\nu_{+}\ll\eta,1/k
.
Suppose
H_{+}
is an
\eta
-intersecting
k
-graph on at most
(1+\nu_{+})n
vertices with vertex set
V_{+}
and edge set
E_{+}
and
H
is a
\varrho
-almost regular induced subgraph of
H_{+}
on
n
vertices.
Then, there is a probabilistic construction of a collection
\mathcal{P}
of
L
-paths in
H
together with a function
\sigma\colon\mathcal{P}\rightarrow[L]_{0}
such that the following holds.

(i)

\lvert\mathcal{P}\rvert\leq\vartheta^{2}n/L
;

(ii)

c=\sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\sigma(P)\geq\vartheta^{4}n
;

(iii)

H-V(\mathcal{P})
is
2\varrho
-almost regular;

(iv)

for all probabilistic constructions of a set
X\subseteq V_{+}
with
X\cap V(\mathcal{P})=\varnothing
and
\lvert X\rvert=c
, there is a probabilistic construction of a collection
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
of paths in
H_{+}
such that the following holds.

(iv.i)

There is a bijection
\varphi:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
such that for all
P\in\mathcal{P}
, the path
\varphi(P)
is an
(L+\sigma(P))
-path with
V(\varphi(P))\subseteq V(P)\cup X
that has the same ordered end-edges as
P
;

(iv.ii)

for all
e\in E_{+}
, we have

\mathds{P}[e\in E(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})]\leq\frac{1}{\vartheta^{4}n^{k-1}}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathds{P}[e\in E(\partial\mathcal{P}^{\prime})]\leq\frac{1}{Ln^{k-1}}.

Proof.

For the probabilistic construction of the collection
\mathcal{P}
together with a function
\sigma
, we will employ Lemma
5.6
. Then, for the probabilistic construction of
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
we will randomly absorb all vertices
x\in X
into the paths in
\mathcal{P}
; that is, we will randomly place every vertex
x\in X
in the center of an
x
-absorber in
H_{+}
that is a subgraph of a path in
\mathcal{P}
.

In more detail, we argue as follows.
Let
E=E(H)
.
For
x\in V_{+}
, let
\mathcal{A}_{x}
denote the set of
x
-absorbers in
H_{+}
.
Choose
\ell
such that
\vartheta\ll\nu_{+},1/\ell\ll\eta,1/k
.
Let
a=1/\vartheta
.
Lemma
5.6
provides a probabilistic construction of a collection
\mathcal{P}
of
L
-paths in
H
together with a set
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathcal{B}^{a,\ell}(P)
such that the following holds.

(1)

\lvert\mathcal{P}\rvert\leq\vartheta^{2}n/L
;

(2)

H-V(\mathcal{P})
is
2\varrho
-almost regular;

(3)

\lvert\{B\in\mathcal{B}\colon\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)\cap\mathcal{A}_{x}\neq\varnothing\}\rvert\geq 3\vartheta^{4}n
for all
x\in V_{+}
;

(4)

\lvert\{x\in V_{+}\colon\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)\cap\mathcal{A}_{x}=\varnothing\}\rvert\leq\vartheta^{4}n
for all
B\in\mathcal{B}
;

(5)

\mathds{P}[e\in E(\mathcal{P})]\leq\vartheta\frac{1}{n^{k-1}}
and
\mathds{P}[e\in E(\partial P)]\leq\frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{n^{k-1}}
for all
e\in E
.

Let
\sigma\colon\mathcal{P}\rightarrow[L]_{0}
with
\sigma(P)=\lvert\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{B}^{a,\ell}(P)\rvert
for all
P\in\mathcal{P}
and let
c=\lvert\mathcal{B}\rvert
. Then
(i)
–
(iii)
hold.

For all
(a,\ell)
-blocks
B
in
H
and all
x\in V_{+}
with
\mathcal{A}_{x}\cap\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)\neq\varnothing
, we fix one
x
-absorber
A_{x}(B)\in\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)
in
H_{+}
for later use.
For
\mathcal{P}
as above and a probabilistic construction of a set
X\subseteq V_{+}
with
X\cap V(\mathcal{P})=\varnothing
and
\lvert X\rvert=c
, we obtain
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
through random absorption of all elements of
X
into the paths in
\mathcal{P}
as follows.
Consider the auxiliary bipartite graph
G
with bipartition
\{X,\mathcal{B}\}
and an edge between
x\in X
and
B\in\mathcal{B}
if and only if
\mathcal{A}_{x}\cap\mathcal{A}^{\ell}(B)\neq\varnothing
. Intuitively, edges in this graph represent possible absorptions of elements of
X
into the adjacent blocks.
Thus, we may think of perfect matchings in
G
as representations of valid stategies for the absorption of all elements of
X
.
Due to
(3)
and
(4)
, we have
d_{G}(x)\geq 3\vartheta^{4}n
for all
x\in X
and
d_{G}(B)\geq c-\vartheta^{4}n
for all
B\in\mathcal{B}
.
Therefore, Observation
5.7
guarantees the existence of a set of
\vartheta^{4}n
edge-disjoint perfect matchings in
G
.
Pick one matching uniformly at random from this set and interpret this matching as a bijection
\mu\colon X\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
.
Let
\varphi
denote the bijection defined on
\mathcal{P}
that maps
P\in\mathcal{P}
to the path obtained from
P
when placing
\mu^{-1}(B)
in the center of
A_{\mu^{-1}(B)}(B)
for all
B\in\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{B}^{a,\ell}(P)
. Let
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}=\Ima(\varphi)
.

It remains to check that this defines a probabilistic construction of a collection
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
of paths satisfying
(iv)(iv.ii)
.
For all
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V_{+}}{k-1}
and all possible realisations
\mathcal{Q}
of
\mathcal{P}
, there is at most one block
B\in\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathcal{B}^{a,\ell}(P)
with
d_{B}(\mathbf{x})\geq 1
.
Hence, for all
x\in V_{+}
and
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V_{+}}{k-1}
, we have

(5.9)

\mathds{P}[x\in X\wedge d_{\mu(x)}(\mathbf{x})\geq 1\mid\mathcal{P},X]\leq\frac{1}{\vartheta^{4}n}

by construction of
\mu
.
Thus, for all
e\in E_{+}
,
(5)
yields

\displaystyle\mathds{P}[e\in E(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})]

\displaystyle\leq\mathds{P}[\mathbf{x}\cap X=\varnothing\wedge e\in E(\mathcal{P})]+\sum_{x\in e}\mathds{P}[x\in X\wedge d_{\mu(x)}(e\smallsetminus\{x\})\geq 1]

\displaystyle\overset{\mathclap{\ref{item: app probability for occurence}}}{\leq}\frac{\vartheta}{n^{k-1}}+\sum_{x\in e}\mathds{P}[x\in X\wedge d_{\mu(x)}(e\smallsetminus\{x\})\geq 1\wedge d_{\mathcal{P}}(e\smallsetminus\{x\})\geq 1]

\displaystyle\overset{\mathclap{\eqref{equation: probability matching x to rest}}}{\leq}\frac{\vartheta}{n^{k-1}}+\sum_{x\in e}\frac{1}{\vartheta^{4}n}\mathds{P}[d_{\mathcal{P}}(e\smallsetminus\{x\})\geq 1]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{\vartheta}{n^{k-1}}+\sum_{x\in e}\frac{1}{\vartheta^{4}n}\sum_{v\in V_{+}}\mathds{P}[(e\smallsetminus\{x\})\cup\{v\}\in E(\mathcal{P})]

\displaystyle\overset{\mathclap{\ref{item: app probability for occurence}}}{\leq}\frac{\vartheta}{n^{k-1}}+j\cdot\frac{1}{\vartheta^{4}n}\cdot(1+\nu_{+})n\cdot\frac{\vartheta}{n^{k-1}}\leq\frac{1}{\vartheta^{4}n^{k-1}}.

Furthermore, we obtain

\mathds{P}[e\in E(\partial\mathcal{P}^{\prime})]=\mathds{P}[e\in E(\partial\mathcal{P})]\leq\frac{1}{L}\frac{1}{n^{k-1}},

which completes the proof.
∎

6.
From paths to cycles

In this section, we perform the step from the yield of Proposition
4.1
to the decomposition into cycle factors as in our main theorem.
We do this by describing a random process which converts one almost spanning path collection into a cycle factor and subsequently using another random process which repeatedly applies the first one to transform path collection after path collection.
The first step is done in Lemma
6.3
and the second in Proposition
6.4
.

We begin with the following somewhat standard lemma, which states that in any
\eta
-intersecting
k
-graph, there is a small (reservoir) set such that between any two ordered edges, there are many short paths with all “inner” vertices in this set.
Complementing the notation
\partial P
, for a path
P=v_{1},\dots,v_{\ell}
, we define the
interior
of
P
as (the subpath)
P^{\circ}=v_{k+1},\dots,v_{\ell-k}
if
\ell\geq 2k+1
and
P^{\circ}=P[\varnothing]
otherwise.
The vertex set of
P^{\circ}
is the set of
inner vertices
of
P
.
For a collection
\mathcal{P}
of paths, we define
\mathcal{P}^{\circ}=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}P^{\circ}
.

Lemma 6.1
.

Suppose
1/n\ll\beta,\varrho\ll 1/\ell_{0},1/\ell_{1}\ll\eta,1/k
, where
\ell_{0}\leq\ell_{1}
.
Suppose
H
is an
\eta
-intersecting
\varrho
-almost regular
k
-graph on
n
vertices with vertex set
V
and edge set
E
.
Then there is a set
R\subseteq V
such that the following holds.

(i)

\beta n/2\leq\lvert R\rvert\leq\beta n
;

(ii)

The next lemma ensures that under the right conditions, many tuples can be connected in a probabilistically well behaved way.
It will later be useful when building the cycle factor in Lemma
6.3
.

Further, for all
i\in[m]
, let
\lambda_{i}\in[\ell_{0},\ell_{1}]
and suppose that
\mathcal{P}_{i}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{4\zeta\ell_{1}^{k}}{\beta n^{k-1}}+2^{k}\cdot\frac{\zeta k^{k}\cdot 2\ell_{1}^{k}}{\beta n^{k-1}}\leq\frac{\zeta^{1/2}}{n^{k-1}}\,,

∎

In the following lemma, we transform a path collection as yielded by Proposition
4.1
into a cycle factor.
It resembles the usual final step in a proof by absorption, in particular, this is where we will use Proposition
5.8
.
However, in order to subsequently apply this construction process multiple times in the proof of Proposition
6.4
without ruining certain quasirandom properties, we need to construct the cycle factor probabilistically and take care that the probability for any edge to occur in the constructed cycle factor is small enough.
Figure
6.1
illustrates this process.

Lemma 6.3
.

Suppose
1/n\ll\mu,1/L\ll\delta\ll\varrho\ll\eta,1/k
.
Suppose
H
is a
k
-graph on
n
vertices with vertex set
V
and
F
is an
\eta
-intersecting
\varrho
-almost regular spanning subgraph of
H
.
Let
\mathcal{P}\subseteq H-F
be a collection of
L
-paths with
|V(\mathcal{P})|\geq(1-\mu)n
and let
\mathcal{C}
be a cycle factor on
n
vertices of girth at least
L^{3}
.

Then, there is a probabilistic construction of a copy
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
of
\mathcal{C}
in
H
such that
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\cup F
and for every
e\in E(F)
of type
\tau\in\mathcal{T}\smallsetminus\{\textup{k-end}\}
, we have
\mathds{P}[e\in E(F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime})]\leq p_{\tau}
, where
p_{1\textup{-con}}=\frac{\delta^{1/2}}{n^{k-1}}
,
p_{j\textup{-end}}=\frac{1}{\delta^{k}n^{k-j}}
for all
j\in[k-1]
, and
p_{j\textup{-con}}=p_{\textup{lo}}=\frac{1}{\delta^{k}n^{k-1}}
for all
j\in[k]\smallsetminus\{1\}
.

Proof.

We use the absorption method to transform the almost spanning collection of paths
\mathcal{P}
into the desired cycle factor
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
.
To this end, we perform the usual steps of a proof via absorption in a
k
-graph similar to
F[V\smallsetminus V(\mathcal{P})]
.
That is, we set aside the absorbing structure (via Proposition
5.8
), cover almost everything (via Proposition
4.1
), connect all the paths in the approximate covering, in the absorbing structure, and, in this case, paths in
\mathcal{P}
(via Lemma
3.11
), and finally, we absorb the remaining vertices.
Note however, that here we actually want to perform all these steps as a probabilistic construction and analyse the probabilities for edges of
F
to occur in
F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
.

Suppose

(6.1)

\displaystyle 1/n\ll\mu,1/L\ll\delta\ll\varrho\ll 1/L^{\prime}\ll\mu^{\prime}\ll\beta\ll\vartheta\ll\ell_{1}\ll\ell_{0}\ll\eta,1/k\,.

We say a set
\hat{\mathcal{P}}\subseteq\mathcal{P}
is
good
if for
\hat{V}=V\smallsetminus V(\hat{\mathcal{P}})
, we have
|\hat{V}|\in[\frac{\delta}{2}n,\frac{3}{2}\delta n]
, for all
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
, we have
|N_{F}(\mathbf{x})\cap N_{F}(\mathbf{y})\cap\hat{V}|\geq\frac{\eta}{2}|\hat{V}|
, and
F[\hat{V}]
is
2\varrho
-almost regular.
Consider a random selection
\mathcal{P}_{\text{rand}}
of paths in
\mathcal{P}
which includes every path in
\mathcal{P}
independently with probability
1-\delta
.
Then McDiarmid’s inequality (Lemma
3.2
) guarantees that
\mathds{P}[\mathcal{P}_{\text{rand}}\text{ is good}]\geq\frac{99}{100}
, say.
Denote the set of good sets by
\mathscr{P}
and pick a set
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}=\{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\}
at random from
\mathscr{P}
such that

{\mathds{P}}[\mathcal{P}^{\prime}=\mathcal{Q}]={\mathds{P}}[\mathcal{P}_{\text{rand}}=\mathcal{Q}\mid\mathcal{P}_{\text{rand}}\in\mathscr{P}]

for all
\mathcal{Q}\in\mathscr{P}
.
Then
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
is good and we set
V_{1}=V\smallsetminus V(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})
.
For
P\in\mathcal{P}
, we have
V(P)\subseteq V_{1}
if and only if
P\notin\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
, and each path in
\mathcal{P}
is included in
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
independently with probability
1-\delta
.
Thus, for distinct
\widetilde{P}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{P}_{k}\in\mathcal{P}
, we have

\displaystyle\mathds{P}\Big[\bigcup_{i\in[k]}V(\widetilde{P}_{i})\subseteq V_{1}\Big]=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathds{P}[\mathcal{P}_{\text{rand}}\in\mathscr{P}\land\forall i\in[k]:\widetilde{P}_{i}\notin\mathcal{P}_{\text{rand}}]}{\mathds{P}[\mathcal{P}_{\textup{rand}}\in\mathscr{P}]}

(6.2)

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle{\mathds{P}}[\forall i\in[k]:\widetilde{P}_{i}\notin\mathcal{P}_{\text{rand}}]\cdot\frac{100}{99}\leq\frac{100\delta^{k}}{99}\,.

Next, we describe the construction of a copy
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
of
\mathcal{C}
and analyse
\mathds{P}[e\in E(F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime})\mid\mathcal{P}^{\prime}]
for all
e\in E
(note that fixing
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
in particular fixes
V_{1}
).
In the end, we use this to deduce the upper bound on the probabilities for different types of edges of
F
to lie in
E(F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime})
.
Since we perform several probabilistic constructions sequentially, in principle, we could obtain all the probabilities conditioned on all previous steps.
However, for our analysis it suffices to condition only on the choice of
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
.

\mathcal{P}
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
P_{i}
\widehat{\mathcal{W}}
\mathcal{S}

is a path in
H
.
Set

U_{i}=V_{1}\smallsetminus\Big(R\cup\bigcup_{i^{\prime}\in[i-1]}u_{i^{\prime}}\cup v_{i^{\prime}}\Big)

and note that since
m\leq\frac{n}{L}
, we know that
|U_{i}|\geq(1-\frac{3}{2}\beta)|V_{1}|
holds.
Moreover, since
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
is good, we know that for all
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
and
U\subseteq V_{1}
with
|U|\geq(1-2\beta)|V_{1}|
, we have

(6.3)

\displaystyle|N_{F}(\mathbf{x})\cap N_{F}(\mathbf{y})\cap U|\geq\frac{\eta}{3}|V_{1}|\quad\text{and}\quad|N_{F}(\mathbf{x})\cap U|\geq\frac{\eta}{3}|V_{1}|\,.

Suppose for some
j\in[k]
, vertices
u_{i}^{j^{\prime}}
are given for all
j^{\prime}\in\{j+1,\dots,k\}
.
Then choose
u_{i}^{j}\in N_{F}(u_{i}^{j+1},\dots,u_{i}^{k},a_{i}^{1},\dots,a_{i}^{j-1})\cap U_{i}
uniformly at random (note that due to (
6.3
), this means that
u_{i}^{j}
is chosen uniformly at random from a set of size at least
\frac{\eta}{3}|V_{1}|
).
Subsequently, suppose that for some
j\in[k]
, vertices
v_{i}^{j^{\prime}}
are given for all
j^{\prime}\in[j-1]
.
Then choose

v_{i}^{j}\in N_{F}(b_{i}^{j+1},\dots,b_{i}^{k},v_{i}^{1},\dots,v_{i}^{j-1})\cap(U_{i}\smallsetminus u_{i})

uniformly at random.
By this definition, the edges
u_{1},v_{1},\dots,u_{m},v_{m}
are pairwise disjoint.

For
j\in[k-1]
and a
j
-ending edge
e\in E(F)
, we consider all partitions
\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2}\}
of
e
for which there exists a
P\in\mathcal{P}
such that
\mathbf{x}_{1}
is an end-set of
P

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}$\cr\vskip 0.0pt\cr$\scriptscriptstyle v$\cr}}}_{i^{\prime}})\Big]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{L^{\prime}}{|V_{1}|^{k-1}}+\frac{\ell_{0}}{|V_{1}|^{k-j}}\leq\frac{1}{\delta^{k}n^{k-j}}\,.

Lastly, if
e\in E(F)
is neither
1
-concentrated nor ending, (
6
) together with (
6.5
), (
6.16
), (
6.17
), and (
6
) entail that

\mathds{P}[e\in E(F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime})]\leq\frac{L^{\prime}}{|V_{1}|^{k-1}}\leq\frac{1}{\delta^{k}n^{k-1}}\,.

Summarised, we provided a probabilistic construction of a cycle factor
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
which is a copy of the cycle factor
\mathcal{C}
such that for every
e\in E(F)
, the probability
\mathds{P}[e\in E(F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime})]
is bounded as claimed in the statement.
∎

The next proposition says that given an approximate decomposition of the edge set into approximate partitions of the vertex set into long paths, that is, given the setup after applying Proposition
4.1
, we can indeed obtain an approximate decomposition of the edge set into given cycle factors of not too small girth.

Proposition 6.4
.

Suppose
1/n\ll 1/L\ll\mu\ll\varrho\ll\eta,1/k
.
Suppose
H
is a
k
-graph on
n
vertices with vertex set
V
and
F
is an
\eta
-intersecting
\varrho
-almost regular spanning subgraph of
H
.
Suppose
\mathcal{P}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{P}_{r}
are edge-disjoint collections of
L
-paths in
H-F
with
|V(\mathcal{P}_{i})|\geq(1-\mu)n
for all
i\in[r]
such that for all
\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}
, we have

(i)

|\mathcal{I}_{\textup{lo}}(\mathbf{e})|\leq\mu r
;

(ii)

|\mathcal{I}_{j\textup{-con}}(\mathbf{e})|\leq 2^{L^{2}}n^{k-j}
for all
j\in[k-1]
and
|\mathcal{I}_{k\textup{-con}}(\mathbf{e})|\leq 2^{L^{2}}n
;

(iii)

|\mathcal{I}_{j\textup{-end}}(\mathbf{e})|\leq\frac{n^{k-j}}{L^{1/2}}
for all
j\in[k-1]
.

Then, for all cycle factors
\mathcal{C}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{r}
on
n
vertices of girth at least
L^{3}
, there are edge-disjoint copies of
\mathcal{C}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{r}
in
H
.

Proof.

In the following, we will analyse a random process in which we utilise Lemma
6.3
to transform each collection of paths
\mathcal{P}_{i}
in a fairly uniform way into a cycle factor
\mathcal{C}_{i}^{\prime}
that is a copy of
\mathcal{C}_{i}
.

Suppose
\mu\ll\delta\ll\varrho
and define a random process inductively as follows.
Suppose that for some
i\in[r]
and all
j\in[i-1]
and
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
, we have defined a cycle factor
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{j}
in
H
and a
\{0,1\}
-valued random variable
Y_{j}^{\mathbf{x}}
.
Further, set
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{<i}=\bigcup_{j\in[i-1]}\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{j}
.

Let
\mathcal{E}_{i}
be the event that for all
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
, we have that
d_{F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{<i}}(\mathbf{x})\leq\delta^{1/4}n
.
If
\mathcal{E}_{i}
does not occur, we set
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{i}=\varnothing
and choose
{Y_{i}^{\mathbf{x}}}_{|\mathcal{E}_{i}^{c}}
such that
\mathds{P}[Y_{i}^{\mathbf{x}}=1\mid(Y^{\mathbf{x}}_{j})_{j\in[i-1]},\mathcal{E}_{i}^{c}]=\sum_{\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}\colon\mathbf{x}\subseteq\mathbf{e}}p_{\tau(\mathbf{e},i)}
.
In the end, we will show that with high probability,
\mathcal{E}_{i}
occurs for all
i\in[r]
.

If
\mathcal{E}_{i}
occurs, it follows that for all
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
, we have

|N_{F-\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{<i}}(\mathbf{x})\cap N_{F-\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{<i}}(\mathbf{y})|\geq|N_{F}(\mathbf{x})\cap N_{F}(\mathbf{y})|-2\delta^{1/4}n\geq\frac{\eta}{2}n

and that
F-\mathcal{C}_{<i}^{\prime}
is
2\varrho
-almost regular.
This means that if
\mathcal{E}_{i}
occurs, we may apply Lemma
6.3
, with
H
,
F-\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{<i}
,
L
,
\mathcal{C}_{i}
,
\mathcal{P}_{i}
,
\eta/2
,
2\varrho
,
\delta
,
\mu
here instead of
H
,
F
,
L
,
\mathcal{C}
,
\mathcal{P}
,
\eta
,
\varrho
,
\delta
,
\mu
there, to obtain a probabilistic construction of a cycle factor
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{i}
in
H
such that

•

\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{i}
is a copy of the cycle factor
\mathcal{C}_{i}
;

•

E(\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{i})\subseteq E(\mathcal{P}_{i})\cup E(F-\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{<i})
(in particular,
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{i}
is edge-disjoint from every cycle factor
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{j}
for all
j\in[i-1]
);

•

\mathds{P}[\mathbf{e}\in E(F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{i})\mid(Y_{j}^{\mathbf{x}})_{j\in[i-1]},\mathcal{E}_{i}]\leq p_{\tau(\mathbf{e},i)}
for every
\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}
where
p_{1\textup{-con}}=\frac{\delta^{1/2}}{n^{k-1}}
,
p_{j\textup{-end}}=\frac{1}{\delta^{k}n^{k-j}}
for all
j\in[k-1]
,
p_{\textup{$k$-end}}=0
, and
p_{j\textup{-con}}=p_{\textup{lo}}=\frac{1}{\delta^{k}n^{k-1}}
for all
j\in[k]\smallsetminus\{1\}
(here
p_{\textup{$k$-end}}=0
holds since if
\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}
is
k
-ending with respect to
\mathcal{P}_{i}
, then
\mathbf{e}\notin E(F)
).

Denoting the indicator variable of the event
d_{F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{i}}(\mathbf{x})\geq 1
by
I^{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
for every
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
, this definition of
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{i}
implies
\mathds{P}[I^{\mathbf{x}}_{i}=1\mid(Y_{j}^{\mathbf{x}})_{j\in[i-1]},\mathcal{E}_{i}]\leq\sum_{\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}\colon\mathbf{x}\subseteq\mathbf{e}}p_{\tau(\mathbf{e},i)}
and we set
{Y^{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}_{|\mathcal{E}_{i}}={I_{i}^{\mathbf{x}}}_{|\mathcal{E}_{i}}
.
Thus, for all
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
, we have

(6.114)

\displaystyle\big|\{i\in[r]\colon d_{F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{i}}(\mathbf{x})\geq 1\}\big|\leq\sum_{i\in[r]}Y_{i}^{\mathbf{x}}\,.

By definition, we have that
\mathds{P}[Y^{\mathbf{x}}_{i}=1\mid(Y^{\mathbf{x}}_{j})_{j\in[i-1]}]\leq\sum_{\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}\colon\mathbf{x}\subseteq\mathbf{e}}p_{\tau(\mathbf{e},i)}
holds for all
i\in[r]
and this entails that for all
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
, we have

\displaystyle\sum_{i\in[r]}{\mathds{E}}\big[Y_{i}^{\mathbf{x}}=1\mid(Y_{j}^{\mathbf{x}})_{j\in[i-1]}\big]\leq\sum_{\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}\colon\mathbf{x}\subseteq\mathbf{e}}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}p_{\tau}|\mathcal{I}_{\tau}(\mathbf{e})|

\displaystyle\overset{\text{\ref{it:leftover}--\ref{it:j-end}}}{\leq}

\displaystyle n\Big(\mu r\cdot\frac{1}{\delta^{k}n^{k-1}}+r\cdot\frac{\delta^{1/2}}{n^{k-1}}+2\sum_{j\in[k-1]\smallsetminus\{1\}}2^{L^{2}}n^{k-j}\frac{1}{\delta^{k}n^{k-1}}+\sum_{j\in[k-1]}\frac{n^{k-j}}{L^{1/2}}\frac{1}{\delta^{k}n^{k-j}}\Big)\leq\frac{\delta^{1/3}n}{2}\,.

Thus, we obtain by Freedman’s inequality (Lemma
3.3
) that

(6.115)

\displaystyle\mathds{P}\Big[\sum_{i\in[r]}Y^{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\geq\delta^{1/3}n\Big]\leq\exp(-n^{1/2})\,.

Suppose now that
\sum_{i\in[r]}Y_{i}^{\mathbf{x}}\leq\delta^{1/3}n
holds for all
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
.
Then by (
6.114
), we conclude that
d_{F\cap\mathcal{C}^{\prime}_{<i}}(\mathbf{x})\leq\delta^{1/4}n
holds for all
i\in[r]
and
\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}
, meaning that the event
\mathcal{E}_{i}
occurs for all
i\in[r]
.
Consequently, by (
6.115
) and the union bound we conclude that

\mathds{P}\Big[\bigcap_{i\in[r]}\mathcal{E}_{i}\Big]\geq\mathds{P}\biggr[\sum_{i\in[r]}Y^{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\leq\delta^{1/3}n\text{ for all }\mathbf{x}\in\binom{V}{k-1}\biggr]>0\,.

Thus, with positive probability it happens that
\mathcal{E}_{i}
occurs for all
i\in[r]
, meaning that in each step
i
of this random process we construct a copy of
\mathcal{C}_{i}
that is edge-disjoint from all previously constructed cycle factors.
This yields edge-disjoint copies of
\mathcal{C}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{r}
, as desired.
∎

7.
Proof of Theorem
1.3

We now prove our main theorem by combining Propositions
4.1
and
6.4
.

Proof of Theorem
1.3
.

Suppose
1/n\ll\varrho,1/L\ll\mu\ll\varrho_{F}\ll\varepsilon\ll\eta,1/k
.
Suppose
H
is an
\eta
-intersecting
\varrho
-almost
r
-regular
k
-graph on
n
vertices. Let
r^{\prime}=(1-\varepsilon)r/k
and suppose
\mathcal{C}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{r^{\prime}}
are cycle factors, whose girth is at least
L
.
We show that there is a suitable spanning subgraph
F
of
H
such that Proposition
4.1
guarantees the existence of collections
\mathcal{P}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{r^{\prime}}
of paths in
H-F
that we can connect to cycles forming a copy of
\mathcal{C}_{i}
for all
i\in[r^{\prime}]
via Proposition
6.4
.

Let
V=V(H)
and
E=E(H)
. Let
F
be a random spanning subgraph of
H
for which every edge
e\in E
is included in
E(F)
independently at random with probability
p=\varepsilon-2\varrho
.
Then Chernoff’s inequality (Lemma
3.1
) and the union bound show that with positive probability
F
is an
\varepsilon^{2}\eta/2
-intersecting
2\varrho
-almost
pr
-regular spanning subgraph of
H
such that
H-F
is
\eta/2
-intersecting.
From now on, let
F
denote such a subgraph.

For all
v\in V
, we have

d_{H^{\prime}}(v)\geq((1-\varrho)-(1+2\varrho)(\varepsilon-2\varrho))r\geq kr^{\prime}

and

d_{H^{\prime}}(v)\leq((1+\varrho)-(1-2\varrho)(\varepsilon-2\varrho))r\leq(1+4\varrho)kr^{\prime}.

Thus with
4\varrho
,
L^{1/3}
,
\eta/2
,
\mu
,
H^{\prime}
playing the roles of
\varrho
,
L
,
\eta
,
\mu
,
H
, Proposition
4.1
yields edge-disjoint collections
\mathcal{P}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{r^{\prime}}
of
L^{1/3}
-paths in
H^{\prime}
with
\lvert V(\mathcal{P}_{i})\rvert\geq(1-\mu)n
for all
i\in[r^{\prime}]
such that the following holds for all
\mathbf{e}\in\binom{V}{k}
.

•

\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\textup{lo}}(\mathbf{e})\rvert\leq\mu r^{\prime}
;

•

\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\textup{$j$-con}}(\mathbf{e})\rvert\leq n^{k-j}/(\eta/2)^{2L^{1/3}}
for all
j\in[k-1]
and
\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\textup{$k$-con}}(\mathbf{e})\rvert\leq n/(\eta/2)^{2L^{1/3}}
;

•

\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\textup{$j$-end}}(\mathbf{e})\rvert\leq n^{k-j}/L^{1/6}
for all
j\in[k-1]
.

Since
F
is
2\varrho
-almost regular,
F
is in particular
\varrho_{F}
-almost regular. Consequently, with
L^{1/3}
,
\mu
,
\varrho_{F}
,
\varepsilon^{2}\eta/2
,
H
,
F
playing the roles of
L
,
\mu
,
\varrho
,
\eta
,
H
,
F
, Proposition
6.4
yields copies of the given cycle factors as desired.
∎

8.
Concluding remarks

In this paper, we prove a strong generalization of both the well-known Dirac-type result for the existence of one Hamilton cycle in large
k
-graphs due to Rödl, Ruciński, and Szemerédi
[
27
,
29
,
28
]
and a result concerning asymptotically optimal packings of Hamilton cycles in graphs by Ferber, Krivelevich, and Sudakov
[
7
]
.
In fact, our result even applies to cycle factors of large girth.

It was recently proved independently by Lang and Sanhueza-Matamala
[
21
]
and by Polcyn, Reiher, Rödl, and Schülke
[
26
]
that every large
k
-graph on
n
vertices with
\delta_{k-2}(H)\geq(5/9+o(1))\binom{n}{2}
contains a Hamilton cycle.
We wonder whether such
k
-graphs actually contain
(1-o(1))\reg_{k}(H)/k
edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles.

There are yet other sufficient conditions for Hamiltonicity in hypergraphs, see for instance
[
31
]
.
It would be interesting to know which other sufficient conditions imply a packing result similar to Theorem
1.1
.
Another tempting question in this direction is as follows.
Call a
k
-graph
H

robustly Hamiltonian
if we can delete
o(n)
edges incident to each
(k-1)
-set and
H
still contains a Hamilton cycle.
Does every large robustly Hamiltonian
k
-graph
H
contain
(1-o(1))\reg_{k}(H)/k
edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles?

Lastly, it would of course be desirable to obtain a real decomposition of a
k
-graph into Hamilton cycles, or even stronger,
to show that any
k
-graph satisfying certain conditions contains
\reg_{k}(H)/k
edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles.
However, even decompositions of cliques into Hamilton cycles are in general not known to exist.
Further, it was recently shown by Piga and Sanhueza-Matamala
[
24
]
that there are arbitrarily large
3
-graphs
H
with
\delta_{2}(H)\geq(\frac{2}{3}-o(1))|V(H)|
which do not contain
\reg_{3}(H)/3
edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles.
Therefore, our results cannot be improved to exact decompositions without increasing the lower bound on the minimum degree significantly.
